opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that if you look at where foundation models have been really successful, in language and in vision, it's been because there was this enormous corpus of data that reflected the thing you actually wanted the model to do. For robotics, that data just doesn't exist on the internet. There's no Wikipedia of robot actions. You can learn a lot from videos of people, and from simulation, and I think those are useful complements, but there's a gap between watching someone fold a shirt and actually having the motor commands, the forces, the feedback from a real gripper interacting with real cloth.

And simulation is great for certain things, but the long tail of the physical world is really hard to model. Deformable objects, cluttered kitchens, the way a cable kind of snags on something. If you try to hand-engineer all of that into a simulator, you end up spending a ton of effort and you still have a sim-to-real gap. So our bet has been that the most direct path is to collect data on real robots, doing real tasks, in a lot of different environments, and across a lot of different robot embodiments.

The embodiment piece is actually pretty important to us. Rather than collecting all our data on one platform, we've been pulling together data from many different kinds of robots: single arms, bimanual setups, mobile manipulators. And what we've seen is that the model gets better when it's trained on that diversity. It learns something more general about physical interaction that transfers.

The other thing I'd say is that real-world data captures what actually matters. When we look at failures, it's often the messy stuff, recovering from a slip, adjusting when something's not where you expected it. You really only see those situations at scale if you're out there in the real world with robots. So for us, real data isn't the only ingredient, but it's the foundation that everything else gets built on top of.

r001.rationale: The response says language models benefited from enormous data corpora, while robotics has no comparable internet resource—“There’s no Wikipedia of robot actions.”

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the simplest way to put it is that there's no internet for robot actions. If you look at what made language models work, it's that there was this enormous corpus of text sitting around that captures a huge fraction of what humans know and how we communicate. For robots, nothing like that exists. There's lots of video of people doing things, and that's useful, but video doesn't tell you what the motor commands were, what the forces were, what it felt like to grasp the object. The data that maps observations to actions in the physical world basically has to be created.

So from the beginning at PI, we viewed data as the central bottleneck, more so than architecture or algorithms. We take a lot of ideas from the rest of machine learning, but the thing that's really unique to our problem is figuring out how to get a large, diverse dataset of robots actually doing things in the real world. That means teleoperating robots in lots of different environments, on lots of different tasks, with lots of different embodiments, and treating that as a first-class part of the research rather than something you do once to set up an experiment.

There's also a question of why real-world data rather than simulation, which comes up a lot. Simulation is great for some things, locomotion especially, where the contacts are relatively simple. But for manipulation, where you're dealing with deformable objects, cluttered kitchens, laundry, things that are hard to model, the gap between sim and reality is still really large. And part of what you want the model to learn is exactly the messy stuff that's hard to simulate. So our view has been that if you want robots that generalize to the real world, the most reliable path is to learn from the real world, and then use pretraining across many tasks and robots so each new thing requires less data than it would from scratch.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the internet-scale text corpus that helped language models with the lack of any comparable resource for robot actions, explaining that real-world observation-to-action data must be created.

astra-6.text:
The core reason is that if we want robots to learn to interact with the physical world, they need experience interacting with the physical world. Internet data can give you a lot of information about what objects look like or how people describe tasks, but it doesn’t directly tell you what happens when a robot takes an action. If you grasp something a little differently, does it slip? If you push on something, does it move? Those are things you need to learn from interaction.

And we want to build models that can generalize across tasks and environments, so the diversity of that experience really matters. You don’t want all your data to be one robot doing one task in one carefully controlled setting. You want variation in objects, environments, and behaviors, so the model can learn things that transfer to a situation it hasn’t seen before.

That’s why collecting real-world data is so central to the approach. It provides the connection between perception and action—between recognizing what’s in front of you and actually being able to do something useful with it.

r001.rationale: The response says internet data does not directly show what happens when a robot acts, so robots need interaction experience. It does not state that robotics lacks a preexisting data resource comparable to internet-scale text for language models.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that we want robots to learn from experience, much like people do. And if you want a robot to operate in the physical world, it needs experience interacting with that world. There’s a lot you can learn from internet images and videos, but they don’t directly tell you what happens when you apply a particular action—how an object moves when you push it, or how much force you need to grasp something.

So collecting real-world robot data gives us that connection between what the robot sees, what it does, and what happens next. And we’re interested in collecting that experience across different tasks, objects, and environments, so that we can train a generalist model that shares knowledge across them. The goal isn’t to collect demonstrations of every possible situation. It’s to get enough diversity that the robot can start generalizing to situations it hasn’t seen before.

r001.rationale: The response says internet images and videos do not reveal action outcomes, but it does not explain that robotics lacks a preexisting data resource comparable to internet-scale text for language models.
